h1: A month of short video content for a brewpub on a small budget
title: A Month of Short Video for a Brewpub | Craft Beer School
desc: A practical four-week short video plan for a brewpub using a phone, real brewery moments and simple editing, within alcohol content rules.
teaser: Steam rising from the mash tun at 7 am is better content than any stock clip. Most brewpubs film nothing of it.
standfirst: Short vertical videos reach more people than photos on most platforms, but many brewpubs post one burst and then stop. Here is a month of simple videos a small team can shoot on a phone, with a plan that keeps going.
sections: Why short video needs a plan

Reels and short videos now get more reach than still posts for many accounts. A brewpub has something most restaurants do not: a working brewery full of movement, steam, foam and noise. That is natural video material.

The problem is consistency. Most brewpubs film three clips in a burst of enthusiasm, then nothing for a month. A simple plan with set days and themes fixes that. The goal is three short videos a week for four weeks, about twelve in total, made with a phone and a free editing app.

• A recent phone with a clean lens. Wipe it before every shoot. Brewhouse steam fogs lenses.
  • A small tripod or clamp for steady shots of pours and brewing.
  • A clip-on microphone if anyone talks to camera. The brewhouse and bar are noisy.
  • Natural light where possible. Shoot near windows or in the late afternoon. Avoid harsh overhead tube lights.

Shoot vertically at 9:16. Keep most videos between 10 and 40 seconds. Put the strongest moment in the first two seconds, because people scroll fast.

Week one: the brewery at work. A mash-in time-lapse with steam rising. The hop addition in slow motion. A brewer explaining in fifteen seconds what they are making today.

Week two: the beer. A perfect pour from tap to glass. A side by side of three beers showing colour from pale to dark. A short "what does it taste like" clip with a staff member describing one beer in plain words.

Week three: the people. Meet the head brewer. A day in the life of a bartender. The chef pairing one beer with one dish from the menu.

Week four: the place and the community. Quiz night highlights with permission from guests. A new beer tapping. A short thank-you video to regulars.

That is twelve videos, each built from real moments you already have. None needs a script longer than three lines.

Brewhouses are hot, wet and full of hazards. Agree with the head brewer when filming is allowed. Never film while someone is handling caustic, opening a pressurised vessel or working at height. Keep the person filming out of walkways and away from hot liquor and steam vents.

The best shots are often the simplest: wort running clear from the lauter tun, the rolling boil, the moment yeast is pitched. These need no talking, just a steady phone and a little patience.

Use a free mobile editing app. Trim each clip tight, add captions for the key words because many people watch on mute. Use trending or royalty-free music from within the platform rather than copyrighted tracks pulled from elsewhere.

Batch the work. Film on two days a week and edit in one sitting. A small team can make a week's videos in about two hours once they have a rhythm.

Our guide to photographing beer for Instagram covers lighting and glassware tips that apply to video as well.

Alcohol content has extra rules. India restricts alcohol advertising. Platforms also have their own policies on alcohol content, including age restrictions you should switch on for your account. Keep videos focused on the craft, the food and the place. Do not show anyone drinking heavily, drinking and driving or anyone who could look underage. Avoid health claims and promises about what beer will do for you. Our guide to alcohol advertising rules in India explains the background.

Get written or recorded permission before featuring customers' faces. Blur anyone who has not agreed.

After four weeks, look at which videos got the most watch time, saves and shares, not just likes. Note which themes and openings held attention. Often the simplest clip, a slow pour or a brewer laughing at a mistake, beats the most polished one.

Keep the themes that worked, drop the ones that did not and plan the next month. The skill that makes the difference is turning video into one part of a wider plan with reviews, search and messaging, so each piece of content supports the others.
faqs: How long should brewpub reels be?
Most work best between 10 and 40 seconds, with the strongest moment in the first two seconds. Shoot vertically at 9:16.
No. A recent phone, a small tripod, a clip-on microphone and good natural light are enough for most brewpub videos.
Can we show people drinking beer in videos?
Keep content responsible and within platform and Indian advertising rules. Focus on craft and food, never show heavy drinking. Get permission before featuring customers.
